title: 2 Samuel 14:1–20
context: Joab, perceiving the king’s heart toward Absalom, sends for a wise woman of Tekoa and gives her a fictional story of a widow whose son killed his brother. Her case draws David into swearing to protect the son, and she then applies it to David’s refusal to bring Absalom home, appealing to God, who “devises means” so that the banished are not outcasts (14:14). David discerns Joab’s hand. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting 14:14 cautiously as a glimpse of God’s mercy without making it a full doctrine.

verses.text: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart was toward Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab perceives that the king’s heart is toward Absalom. What that means for David’s feelings is not spelled out; the verse begins Joab’s initiative.

Arminian readers see Joab acting on what he observes, for reasons of his own and the kingdom’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joab reads the king’s mind and decides to act. His motives are not stated.

Reformed readers see a shrewd servant shaping events in a divided royal house. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without assuming more about Joab’s intentions than the text says.

verses.text: Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there, and said to her, “Please act like a mourner, and put on mourning clothing, please, and don’t anoint yourself with oil; but be as a woman who has mourned a long time for the dead.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab brings a wise woman from Tekoa and tells her to dress and act as a long-grieving mourner. The scheme involves a staged story.

Arminian readers note that the narrative reports the pretense without endorsing it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joab chooses a woman known for wisdom. Tekoa was a town in Judah, later the home of Amos (Amos 1:1).

Reformed readers see human craft used to move the king. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, narrating the scheme rather than commending deception.

verses.text: Go in to the king and speak like this to him.” So Joab put the words in her mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab tells her to go to the king and puts the words in her mouth. The plan is his.

Arminian readers see Joab using an intermediary to influence the king indirectly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The method recalls Nathan’s parable in chapter 12, where a story led David to judge himself. Here it is Joab’s scheme rather than a prophet’s word.

Reformed readers note the difference in source. Both traditions read this as shared ground, observing the parallel without equating the two.

verses.text: When the woman of Tekoa spoke to the king, she fell on her face to the ground, showed respect, and said, “Help, O king!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman of Tekoa falls on her face before the king and cries, “Help, O king!” She appeals for justice.

Arminian readers see the king approached as the protector of the vulnerable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her plea casts David in the role of judge. The appeal is formal and urgent.

Reformed readers see the king’s responsibility to defend widows and the weak. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the situation she will describe is crafted to resemble David’s own dilemma.

verses.text: The king said to her, “What ails you?” She answered, “Truly I am a widow, and my husband is dead.
verses.arminianNotes:
Asked what troubles her, she says she is a widow whose husband is dead. Widows were especially vulnerable.

Arminian readers see the story designed to awaken the king’s compassion for someone with no one else to defend her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her status as a widow places her under the king’s special care. The law repeatedly names widows among the vulnerable (for example, Deuteronomy 24:17).

Reformed readers see a just appeal shaped by Joab’s plan. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Your servant had two sons; and they both fought together in the field, and there was no one to part them, but the one struck the other and killed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
She says her two sons fought in the field, with no one to separate them, and one killed the other. The story echoes Cain and Abel.

Arminian readers see a tragic case designed to parallel Absalom’s killing of Amnon.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fight in the field recalls Genesis 4:8. The parallel to David’s family is clear to the reader.

Reformed readers see a story that draws David toward mercy for a son who killed his brother. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the differences from Absalom’s planned murder.

verses.text: Behold, the whole family has risen against your servant, and they say, ‘Deliver him who struck his brother, that we may kill him for the life of his brother whom he killed, and so destroy the heir also.’ Thus they would quench my coal which is left, and would leave to my husband neither name nor remainder on the surface of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The family demands the surviving son be put to death, which would leave her husband no name or descendant. She calls him her last ‘coal.’

Arminian readers see justice and mercy in tension within the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
The avenger’s claim (compare Numbers 35) would end the family line. Her image of a coal being quenched is vivid.

Reformed readers see a real dilemma between punishment and preservation. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the parallel with Absalom is imperfect, since his act was premeditated.

verses.text: The king said to the woman, “Go to your house, and I will give a command concerning you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king tells her to go home, and he will issue a command for her. David begins to respond.

Arminian readers see compassion moving David toward a protective ruling, though he has not yet committed himself fully.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s reply is cautious and general. The woman will press for more.

Reformed readers see the king being led step by step. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting how the woman seeks a firmer commitment before revealing her purpose.

verses.text: The woman of Tekoa said to the king, “My lord, O king, may the iniquity be on me, and on my father’s house; and may the king and his throne be guiltless.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman asks that any guilt be on her and her father’s house, and that the king and his throne be guiltless. She offers to bear the risk.

Arminian readers see her removing obstacles to a merciful decision.
verses.reformedNotes:
She addresses concern that mercy might involve the king in bloodguilt. Her offer is formal.

Reformed readers see the seriousness of bloodguilt in Israel’s law. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the careful, persuasive structure of her appeal.

verses.text: The king said, “Whoever says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will not bother you any more.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king says that anyone who troubles her should be brought to him, and he will not bother her again. His protection grows firmer.

Arminian readers see David moving from general reassurance to a concrete promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
David commits to defend her personally. The woman has gained more ground.

Reformed readers see persuasion working on the king’s sense of justice and mercy. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, preparing for the oath she seeks in verse 11.

verses.text: Then she said, “Please let the king remember the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She asks the king to remember the LORD so the avenger will not destroy her son; David swears, “As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.” She secures an oath.

Arminian readers see David freely committing himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
The oath in the LORD’s name binds David. The woman now turns to her real purpose.

Reformed readers see the weight of an oath before God. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the irony that David has sworn protection in a case meant to mirror his own.

verses.text: Then the woman said, “Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king.” He said, “Say on.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman asks permission to speak another word to the king, and he tells her to speak. She now turns from her story to David himself.

Arminian readers see a careful transition from parable to application.
verses.reformedNotes:
Having secured the oath, she moves to the real issue. The king allows it.

Reformed readers see the structure resembling Nathan’s ‘You are the man’ in 12:7, though here the speaker is Joab’s agent. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground.

verses.text: The woman said, “Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in speaking this word the king is as one who is guilty, in that the king does not bring home again his banished one.
verses.arminianNotes:
She asks why David has devised such a thing against God’s people, since by his ruling he condemns himself for not bringing home his banished son. She applies the story.

Arminian readers see David being invited to apply his own mercy consistently.
verses.reformedNotes:
The woman turns David’s judgment back on him. His refusal to recall Absalom affects the whole people.

Reformed readers see the persuasive force of her argument. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the argument presses mercy while setting aside the question of justice for Amnon’s murder.

verses.text: For we must die, and are like water spilled on the ground, which can’t be gathered up again; neither does God take away life, but devises means, that he who is banished not be an outcast from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“We must die, and are like water spilled on the ground,” she says; God does not take away life, but devises means that the banished one not be an outcast from him. She appeals to God’s mercy.

Arminian readers, cautiously, see a hint of God’s merciful purpose to restore.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her words speak of God making a way back for the banished. She uses them to support her plea.

Reformed readers likewise see a glimpse of God’s restoring mercy, which Christians find fulfilled in Christ, without making her argument a full doctrine. Both traditions treat this cautiously as shared ground.

verses.text: Now therefore, seeing that I have come to speak this word to my lord the king, it is because the people have made me afraid. Your servant said, ‘I will now speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.’
verses.arminianNotes:
She explains that she came because the people made her afraid, hoping the king would grant her request. She returns to her cover story.

Arminian readers see her shifting between her story and the real issue with skill.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her speech blends the fictional case with the public concern about Absalom. The boundaries are deliberately blurred.

Reformed readers see rhetorical wisdom at work. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without endorsing the pretense but recognizing the woman’s skill in Joab’s scheme.

verses.text: For the king will hear, to deliver his servant out of the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together out of the inheritance of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
She says the king will rescue her from the man who would destroy her and her son from the inheritance of God. The inheritance theme appears.

Arminian readers see concern for keeping families within God’s people and land.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘The inheritance of God’ refers to Israel and its land. Losing an heir means being cut off from it.

Reformed readers see the covenant setting of her plea. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting how she connects a family matter to the people of God.

verses.text: Then your servant said, ‘Please let the word of my lord the king bring rest; for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad. May the LORD, your God, be with you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
She hopes the king’s word will bring rest, saying he is like an angel of God in discerning good and bad, and blesses him. Flattery and hope mix.

Arminian readers see her appealing to David’s best qualities.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her comparison of David to an angel of God is praise, possibly with an element of flattery. She ends with a blessing.

Reformed readers see persuasive speech, not a theological statement about the king. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without overreading the comparison.

verses.text: Then the king answered the woman, “Please don’t hide anything from me that I ask you.” The woman said, “Let my lord the king now speak.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king asks her not to hide anything he asks; she invites him to speak. David senses something more.

Arminian readers see David beginning to perceive the scheme behind the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s request signals suspicion. The woman agrees to answer.

Reformed readers see the king’s discernment emerging. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, preparing for the question about Joab in the next verse.

verses.text: The king said, “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?” The woman answered, “As your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has spoken; for your servant Joab urged me, and he put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks whether Joab’s hand is in this, and she admits that Joab urged her and put the words in her mouth. The truth comes out.

Arminian readers see honesty finally offered when directly asked.
verses.reformedNotes:
David discerns Joab’s influence. The woman confirms it with flattery about the king’s insight.

Reformed readers see the scheme exposed. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the narrative presents both Joab’s plan and its discovery without commending the deception.

verses.text: Your servant Joab has done this thing to change the face of the matter. My lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all things that are on the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She says Joab did this to change the face of the matter, and that the king is wise like an angel of God. Joab’s purpose is named.

Arminian readers see Joab’s aim to shift David’s stance toward Absalom.
verses.reformedNotes:
The woman explains Joab’s motive in general terms. She again praises David’s wisdom.

Reformed readers see human strategy seeking to influence the king. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting that the outcome will reveal whether this change of approach brings real reconciliation.
